transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Um, I'm here because I've been really struggling with these uncontrollable urges to repeat certain behaviors. Mostly, I feel this intense, constant need to wash my hands and clean things over and over again. It's gotten to the point where I just can't stop, and I really need some help.
Before you wash or clean, do you get unwanted thoughts or fears—like feeling contaminated or that something bad will happen if you don’t do it?

Yes, absolutely. I constantly get these overwhelming thoughts that everything around me is covered in germs and that I'm contaminated. The anxiety gets so intense that I feel forced to wash my hands and clean over and over just to make that feeling go away.
About how much time do these washing and cleaning rituals take each day, and are they interfering with work, school, or relationships?

To be honest, I'm not really sure of the exact amount of time it takes up each day, as I tend to lose track of time when I'm doing it. I also haven't really thought about how much it interferes with my daily activities yet, though it definitely feels like a lot.
Do you recognize that these fears about germs and the need to wash are excessive or unreasonable, or do they feel completely true to you?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really thought about whether the fears are reasonable or not. I just feel this overwhelming urge to do them, and it's hard to think about anything else in the moment.
How long have you been having these contamination fears and washing rituals, and did they start suddenly or build up over time?
I'm not exactly sure how long this has been going on or how it first started. I just know that these washing rituals have become a major part of my day and I can't seem to stop doing them.
If you try to resist washing or touching things you think are dirty, what happens—do you feel very anxious, and do you avoid certain places or objects because of this?

Yes, trying to resist the urge to wash makes me feel incredibly anxious and overwhelmed. Because of that, I actively avoid places like public restrooms and try not to touch door handles to prevent contamination and avoid those exhausting rituals altogether.
Besides contamination and washing, do you also have other unwanted thoughts or repeated behaviors, like checking, counting, arranging, or needing things to feel just right?

Yes, I do experience those behaviors quite a bit. I feel compelled to repeatedly check door locks and switches, and I have to arrange objects on my desk in a very precise order to feel comfortable. I also find myself counting in my head and repeating certain actions a specific number of times.
Have you ever had repeated movements or sounds you couldn’t control, like blinking, throat clearing, facial grimacing, or shoulder shrugging?
No, I haven't experienced those kinds of uncontrollable movements or sounds. I don't have any issues with things like blinking or throat clearing.
Can you give me one example of how these rituals have affected your daily life, like making you late, causing skin irritation, or creating problems at work, school, or home?
I'm not quite sure, to be honest. I haven't really thought about how to describe the impact these rituals have on my daily routine yet.
When you wash, check, or count, do you do these to prevent something bad from happening or to relieve anxiety, even if it doesn’t fully make sense to you?

Yes, absolutely. I do those things to prevent terrible things from happening, like getting contaminated or facing some kind of danger, and it's the only way to ease my overwhelming anxiety. Even though I realize deep down that these rituals probably seem excessive and don't make complete sense, I just feel forced to do them anyway.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent intrusive contamination fears and other unwanted thoughts, along with compulsive washing, cleaning, checking, arranging, counting, and repeating behaviors performed to reduce anxiety and prevent feared harm. The symptoms are experienced as difficult to control and at least partially excessive, which strongly supports Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. Duration and clear functional impairment were not fully quantified in the interview, but the syndrome described is most consistent with OCD.
